title: Determinate structures-1
summary: Trusses dominate this subchapter. The determinacy relation m = 2j − 3 and the ability to spot zero-force members are worth more marks than any lengthy joint analysis. Method of joints suits a whole truss, method of sections a few named members — knowing which to reach for is half the skill. For arches and cables, note that the horizontal thrust wL²/8h is the same expression in both, because a cable is an inverted arch, and that a three-hinged arch is determinate precisely because the moment at the crown hinge is zero.

sections.heading: Trusses — determinacy and stability
sections.body:
A **truss** is an assembly of straight members connected at their ends, carrying load by **axial force only**. That idealisation rests on three assumptions:

1. Members are joined by **frictionless pins** (so no moment is transmitted).
2. Loads and reactions are applied **only at the joints**.
3. Member **centroidal axes meet at the joint** (no eccentricity).

Real trusses are bolted or welded, so some moment does develop — the resulting **secondary stresses** are neglected in analysis but are the reason gusset plates are detailed carefully. A load applied **between** joints, such as a purlin resting on the middle of a rafter, produces genuine **bending** in that member and must be treated separately.

**Determinacy of a plane truss:**

> **m = 2j − 3**

where m is the number of members and j the number of joints (the 3 being the minimum reaction components).

| Condition | Classification |
|---|---|
| **m < 2j − 3** | **Deficient / unstable** — a mechanism |
| **m = 2j − 3** | **Perfect — statically determinate** |
| **m > 2j − 3** | **Redundant — statically indeterminate** |

For a **space** truss the relation is **m = 3j − 6**.

The general form, allowing for more than three reactions, is **D_s = m + r − 2j**, with r the number of reaction components.

**A caution:** satisfying m = 2j − 3 is **necessary but not sufficient** for stability. A truss can have the right member count yet be **improperly arranged** — for example with four members forming a rectangle in one panel while another panel has two diagonals. Such a truss is **partially unstable**, and the arithmetic will not reveal it. The physical check is that **every panel must be triangulated**, because the triangle is the only polygon that is rigid without moment-resisting joints.

**Analysis — choosing the method:**

| Method | Use when | Requires |
|---|---|---|
| **Method of joints** | Forces in **all** or most members are wanted | A joint with **not more than 2 unknowns** |
| **Method of sections** | Forces in a **few named** members are wanted | A cut through **not more than 3** unknown members |
| Method of tension coefficients | Systematic, suits computation | — |
| Graphical (Maxwell diagram) | Historical; visual | — |

**Method of sections is the one to reach for** when a question asks for the force in one interior member of a large truss — cutting through it and taking moments about a convenient point gives the answer in a single equation, where the method of joints would require working through half the truss.

**Zero-force members** can be identified by inspection, and doing so saves a great deal of work:

| Configuration | Result |
|---|---|
| **Two** members at an **unloaded** joint, not collinear | **Both are zero-force** |
| **Three** members at an unloaded joint, **two collinear** | The **third (non-collinear) member is zero-force** |
| Two members and an external load **along one** of them | The **other** is zero-force |

Zero-force members are not useless: they **prevent buckling** of long compression members, provide stability during erection, and carry load under a **different** loading case. A question asking "which members carry no force" is asking for the inspection rules above.

**Force sense.** In a roof truss under gravity load: the **top chord (rafter) is in COMPRESSION**, the **bottom chord (tie) is in TENSION**, and — the most-missed item — in a **king post truss the king post is in TENSION**. It does not hold the ridge up; it **hangs the tie beam** from the apex so the long tie does not sag under its own weight and the ceiling load. Calling it a post is misleading; it acts as a hanger.

**Common truss types**, by name:

| Truss | Character |
|---|---|
| **King post** | One central vertical; spans to **8 m** |
| **Queen post** | Two verticals; **8–12 m** |
| **Fink (French)** | Efficient for roofs, W-shaped web |
| **Howe** | Diagonals in compression |
| **Pratt** | **Diagonals in tension** — efficient in steel, since tension members can be slender |
| **Warren** | Alternating diagonals, no verticals |
| **Parker / Bowstring** | Curved top chord following the moment diagram |

The **Pratt versus Howe** distinction is examinable and has a real basis: in a Pratt truss the **long diagonals are in tension** and the short verticals in compression, which suits steel because a tension member's capacity does not depend on its length. A Howe truss reverses this, which suited **timber**, where the long diagonals could be sized for compression and the short verticals made of iron rods in tension.

sections.heading: Arches
sections.body:
An **arch** carries load principally in **compression**, which is why it is the natural form for **masonry and stone** — materials with negligible tensile strength.

**Its defining feature is the HORIZONTAL THRUST at the supports.** A beam produces only vertical reactions; an arch produces vertical **and** horizontal ones, and the horizontal thrust must be absorbed by:

- a sufficient mass of **abutment**;
- a **tie** between the springings (a tied arch or bowstring girder); or
- an **adjacent arch** thrusting back (which is why a row of arches needs substantial **end** piers even though the intermediate ones are slender).

**Determinacy:**

| Arch | Unknowns | Determinacy |
|---|---|---|
| **Three-hinged** | 4 reactions, but M = 0 at the crown hinge | **Determinate** |
| **Two-hinged** | 4 | Indeterminate to **1st** degree |
| **Fixed (hingeless)** | 6 | Indeterminate to **3rd** degree |

The **three-hinged arch is determinate precisely because of the crown hinge**, which supplies the fourth equation **M_crown = 0**. That single condition is the whole method: take moments of one half of the arch about the crown hinge to find H directly.

**Horizontal thrust** for a three-hinged parabolic arch of span L and rise h:

> **UDL w over the whole span: H = w L² / (8 h)**
> **Central point load W: H = W L / (4 h)**

**Note the inverse dependence on the rise.** A **flatter arch thrusts harder** — halving the rise doubles the thrust. That is the fundamental trade-off in arch design: a shallow arch is elegant and reduces the height of approach embankments, but demands far more substantial abutments. It is also why the failure of an arch bridge usually begins with **abutment movement** rather than with the arch ring itself.

**Bending moment in an arch:**

> **M = M_beam − H y**

where M_beam is the moment a simply supported beam of the same span would carry and y is the arch rise at that section. The term **H y** is the relief the arch provides.

**If the arch profile follows the shape of the beam moment diagram**, then M_beam = H y everywhere and the bending moment is **zero throughout** — the arch is in **pure compression**. Such a shape is the **funicular** or **theoretical arch**:

| Loading | Ideal arch shape |
|---|---|
| **UDL along the SPAN** | **Parabola** |
| **UDL along the ARCH** (self weight) | **Catenary** |
| Point loads | A polygon of the funicular shape |

That is why masonry bridge arches approximate a parabola or catenary, and why a **linear arch** or **line of thrust** analysis asks whether the actual thrust line stays **within the middle third** of the arch ring — the same no-tension rule as for a dam.

**Effects to consider in a two-hinged or fixed arch**, since it is indeterminate: **rib shortening** (axial compression shortens the arch, reducing H), **temperature change** (a rise increases H in a fixed arch), **shrinkage**, and **yielding of the abutments** (which reduces H). A **three-hinged arch is immune to all of these**, because it can accommodate the movement without developing stress — which is its practical advantage where foundation settlement is a risk.

sections.heading: Cables and suspension structures
sections.body:
A **cable** carries load in **pure tension** and, having no flexural stiffness, takes up the **funicular shape** of whatever load it carries — the exact mirror of the ideal arch.

| Loading | Cable shape |
|---|---|
| **UDL along the SPAN** (a suspension bridge deck) | **Parabola** |
| **UDL along the CABLE** (self weight, a transmission line) | **Catenary** |
| Point loads | A funicular polygon |

In practice a suspension bridge cable is treated as **parabolic**, because the deck load dominates the cable's own weight.

**Horizontal tension** — note that it is the **same expression as the arch thrust**, for exactly the same reason:

> **H = w L² / (8 h)**

with h the **sag**. A cable is an **inverted arch**: the arch carries the same load in compression and the cable in tension, and the horizontal reaction is identical.

**H is constant along the cable**, because there is no horizontal load. The vertical component varies, so:

> **Tension at any point: T = √(H² + V²)**
> **Maximum tension occurs AT THE SUPPORTS**, where the slope is steepest
> **Minimum tension occurs at the lowest point**, where T = H

So the cable is sized for the tension at the support, and the anchorage must resist both H and V there.

**Length of a parabolic cable** with sag h and span L:

> **L_cable ≈ L (1 + 8h²/(3L²) − 32h⁴/(5L⁴) + …)**

The first two terms are sufficient for the usual shallow sags. A useful consequence: for a sag of L/10, the cable is only about **2.7% longer** than the span — which is why sag has such a large effect on tension but so little on cable length.

**The sag–tension trade-off** is the central design decision:

| Larger sag | Smaller sag |
|---|---|
| **Lower cable tension** (H ∝ 1/h) | Higher tension, more cable steel |
| **Taller towers** | Shorter towers |
| Longer hangers | — |
| More clearance needed below | Flatter, more usable profile |

Typical suspension bridge sag ratios are **h/L = 1/8 to 1/12**. For a **transmission line**, the same trade-off appears as sag against tower height and conductor clearance, with the added complication that sag **varies with temperature and ice load**.

**Supports at different levels** require the low point of the cable to be located first, by resolving the geometry — the two halves then behave as separate parabolas sharing the same H.

**Suspension bridge components** and their duties:

| Component | Duty |
|---|---|
| **Main cables** | Carry the whole load in **tension** to the towers and anchorages |
| **Towers** | Carry the vertical component in **compression** to the foundations |
| **Anchorages** | Resist the **horizontal** component — massive gravity or rock anchors |
| **Hangers (suspenders)** | Transfer deck load to the cables |
| **Stiffening girder / truss** | **Distributes concentrated loads** and resists **aerodynamic instability** |

The **stiffening girder** deserves emphasis. A bare cable-and-deck system has almost no torsional or flexural stiffness, so a moving load produces large local deflections and wind can excite **flutter** — the mechanism that destroyed the Tacoma Narrows bridge in 1940. The stiffening truss both spreads concentrated loads and raises the torsional frequency out of the range wind can excite. That is why modern long-span decks are deep box girders or open trusses, and why aerodynamic testing is now part of the design.

**Relevance in Nepal.** Cable structures are not exotic here but everyday infrastructure: **suspension and suspended footbridges** are the standard river crossing in the hills, built to Department of Local Infrastructure standard designs. The distinction between the two is worth knowing — in a **suspension** bridge the deck hangs from the cables by hangers and the deck is level; in a **suspended** bridge the deck sits **directly on the cables**, which is cheaper and simpler but gives a sagging walkway. Both are analysed with the relations above.

formulas.label: Truss determinacy
formulas.expression: plane: m = 2j − 3 ;   space: m = 3j − 6 ;   general D_s = m + r − 2j
formulas.note: Necessary but NOT sufficient — every panel must also be triangulated.

formulas.label: Zero-force member rules
formulas.expression: Two non-collinear members at an unloaded joint: both zero. Three with two collinear: the third is zero.
formulas.note: They still prevent buckling and carry load under other load cases.

formulas.label: Three-hinged arch — horizontal thrust
formulas.expression: UDL: H = wL²/(8h) ;   central point load: H = WL/(4h)
formulas.note: Determinate because M = 0 at the crown hinge. A FLATTER arch thrusts harder (H ∝ 1/h).

formulas.label: Bending moment in an arch
formulas.note: Zero throughout if the arch follows the beam moment diagram — the funicular shape.

formulas.label: Cable horizontal tension
formulas.note: Identical to the arch thrust, because a cable is an inverted arch. H is constant along the cable.

formulas.label: Cable tension at a point
formulas.expression: T = √(H² + V²) ;   maximum at the SUPPORTS, minimum (= H) at the lowest point
formulas.note: The cable is sized for the support tension; the anchorage resists both H and V.

formulas.label: Length of a parabolic cable
formulas.note: For h/L = 1/10 the cable is only ~2.7% longer than the span.

formulas.label: Ideal (funicular) shapes
formulas.expression: UDL along the SPAN → parabola.   UDL along the MEMBER (self weight) → catenary.
formulas.note: Applies to both arches (compression) and cables (tension).
